name: Tallgrass prairie
notes: Warm-season C4 bunchgrasses 1-3 m tall with forbs, fire-maintained, trees only as bur-oak savanna edges; North American Great Plains east (Iowa, Kansas, Illinois) with Pampas/Eurasian meadow-steppe analogues.

canopy.name: Bur oak
canopy.source: Quercus macrocarpa, central/eastern N America, fire-tolerant savanna oak, 15-30 m — USDA PLANTS / Flora of North America

traits.native_range: Quercus macrocarpa, central/eastern N America, fire-tolerant savanna oak, 15-30 m — USDA PLANTS / Flora of North America
traits.leaf_shape: simple or compound broad leaves, most deciduous in cold bands
traits.trunk: single trunk dividing into a rounded crown
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: huge broad crown on a stout furrowed trunk

growth.juvenile_note: Hypogeal: the acorn stays in the soil and the seedling puts most of its energy into a taproot (1.4 m deep in the first year) while the shoot is small with a few wavy-lobed leaves. Sapling twigs often grow corky ridges. On prairie edges, fire-killed tops resprout from the root for decades ('grubs') before one stem escapes as a slender sapling.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (seed-bearing from ~35 yr, best 75-150; good crops every 2-3 yr; ~30% germinate within a month of seedfall; first-year roots 1.37 m; height growth 0.09-0.52 m/yr; lifespan 200-300 yr; to 52 m); USDA FEIS (remnants 300-400 yr, one ~440; shade-intolerant)

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics and FEIS Quercus macrocarpa (flowers Apr to mid-Jun; acorns ripen in one season and drop Aug-Nov; 0.9 g in Minnesota to 7.5 g and 5 cm in Texas, with a deep fringed cup covering a third or more; large crops in most years, every 2-3 yr); per-tree crop estimated

canopy.name: Plains cottonwood
canopy.source: Populus deltoides ssp. monilifera, N American plains along streams, 15-30 m — USDA PLANTS

traits.leaf_shape: simple or compound broad leaves, most deciduous in cold bands
traits.trunk: single trunk dividing into a rounded crown
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: massive trunk forking high into a broad crown

growth.juvenile_note: Cottony seed germinates within 24-48 h on wet, bare sandbars and mud flats; the seedling has two minute cotyledons and grows slowly for about 3 weeks, then very fast. Dense, even-aged thickets of slender single-stemmed whips form along river bars, with large triangular, coarsely toothed leaves on flattened stalks that flutter; saplings add 1.5-3.5 m a year on good sites.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 2 (P. deltoides: germination within 48 h; slow first 3 weeks then very rapid; seed from 5-10 yr, plains ~10 yr; 1.8-3.7 m/yr; very intolerant of shade; short-lived, 80-90 yr); USDA FEIS (eastern 100-200 yr, plains ~90 yr; 3-58 m tall).

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics vol. 2 (flowers Feb-Apr east, Apr-May plains, before leaves; male catkins 8-13 cm, female 15-30 cm; 3-4-valved capsules with 30-60 seeds ripen in 30-60 days; up to 48 million seeds per tree; wind pollinated); FEIS (capsules 0.8-1.5 cm). Colour is the red male catkins.

canopy.name: Eastern redcedar
canopy.source: Juniperus virginiana, eastern North America, dense conical evergreen 8-18 m that invades unburned prairie and limestone glades — USDA Silvics Manual / Flora of North America / Kew POWO

leaf.note: appressed scale leaves on adult shoots; sharp spreading needle leaves 5-10 mm on juveniles and shade shoots

canopy.silhouette: dense dark green cone, often rusty in winter

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings carry only sharp, spreading, blue-green juvenile needles in fours or pairs and make a soft prickly little cone; scale leaves take over on the upper shoots within a few years, though juvenile foliage persists on shaded and vigorous shoots. Birds drop the seeds along fence rows and under perch trees, so young cedars come up in lines across old pasture and unburned prairie.
growth.source: USDA Silvics Manual Juniperus virginiana (seed-bearing from ~10 yr, best 25-75 yr; most seed germinates the second spring after ripening; typically 9-18 m; intolerant of shade; very old trees on Missouri and Ozark bluffs). Height-age curve estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics Manual Juniperus virginiana (dioecious; pollen shed late winter to spring; berry-like cones 3-7 mm, dark blue with a white bloom, ripen in one season Sep-Nov and hang into winter, eaten and spread by cedar waxwings and other birds). Crop estimated.

bark.notes: thin reddish-brown bark shredding in long fibrous strips; fluted trunk base

leaf.notes: tiny overlapping dark green scales on four-sided twigs; turns rusty bronze-green in winter

flower.form: tiny golden-brown pollen cones at the twig tips in late winter (male trees)

fruit.form: dark blue frosted berry-like cones 4-7 mm crowding the twigs of female trees

appearance.silhouette: narrow dark green cone standing alone in prairie grass
appearance.refs: USDA Silvics Manual; Flora of North America vol. 2; Kew POWO

canopy.name: Common hackberry
canopy.source: Celtis occidentalis, central and eastern North America, 9-25 m tree of prairie stream woods, ravines and bur-oak edges, bark with corky warts and ridges — USDA Silvics Manual / Kew POWO

leaf.note: lopsided base, three main veins from the base, rough sandpapery upper side

canopy.silhouette: rounded crown on a trunk of corky warts

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two notched, rounded cotyledons, then rough, lopsided, toothed leaves on a thin zig-zag stem. Young trees are slender and shade-tolerant, growing up under elms and oaks; the smooth grey bark of a sapling soon breaks out in the corky warts and narrow ridges that mark the species.
growth.source: USDA Silvics Manual Celtis occidentalis (seed-bearing from ~15 yr, optimum 30-70; most seed germinates the spring after dispersal after cold stratification; usually 9-25 m; tolerant of shade; seldom lives over ~150-200 yr). Height-age curve estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics Manual Celtis occidentalis (small greenish flowers with the leaves Apr-May, wind-pollinated; drupes 7-10 mm, orange-red to dark purple, thin sweet pulp, ripen Sep-Oct and hang through winter, eaten by birds and mammals). Crop estimated.

bark.notes: grey bark covered in corky warts and short wing-like ridges

leaf.notes: lopsided ovate leaves with a long tip, toothed, rough above; often curled by nipple galls

flower.form: inconspicuous greenish flowers with the new leaves

fruit.form: pea-sized dark purple drupes on long stalks, hanging through winter

appearance.silhouette: round-crowned tree with warty grey trunk in a prairie ravine
appearance.refs: USDA Silvics Manual; Flora of North America; Kew POWO

shrub.name: Leadplant
shrub.source: Amorpha canescens, Great Plains tallgrass prairie, deep-rooted legume shrub 0.5-1 m — USDA PLANTS

traits.native_range: Amorpha canescens, Great Plains tallgrass prairie, deep-rooted legume shrub 0
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

shrub.silhouette: low grey-leaved shrub with purple spikes

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: two oval cotyledons, then small pinnate leaves with a few grey-hairy leaflets on a thin stem; it pours its energy into a taproot and stays only a few cm tall for a year or two, dying back to the root crown in drought and resprouting. It becomes a low, many-stemmed subshrub with dense, feathery, silvery-grey ('lead-coloured') leaves, topped from about year 3 by spikes of purple flowers.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Amorpha canescens: germination needs >20 C, peaks at ~20 d; seedlings die back to the root crown in drought and resprout; plants 0.3-1.1 m; roots 2-6 m deep; tolerates partial shade but prefers open sites. First flowering age and lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS Amorpha canescens: up to 30 flowering stems and 3,000 flowers per plant, 200-300 per raceme; flowers late Jun-Aug in the north, fruit mature Aug-Sep; solitary bees and beetles main pollinators, honeybees too; hairy indehiscent one-seeded legume, seed ~2 mm. Fruit set, hang and rot times estimated.

shrub.name: Prairie rose
shrub.source: Rosa arkansana, central N America prairies, low suckering shrub to 0.6 m — USDA PLANTS

traits.native_range: Rosa arkansana, central N America prairies, low suckering shrub to 0
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling with 2 small oval cotyledons and a first leaf of 1-3 leaflets, then pinnate leaves of 7-11 toothed leaflets on a thin bristly stem. It becomes a low patch of prickly stems 10-50 cm tall that die back to near the base each winter and resprout, flowering on the new shoots; deep roots (3 m+) send up new stems nearby.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Rosa arkansana (stems 10-50 cm, die back yearly; roots 2.4-3.7 m deep; flowering May-Aug, ~33 days per population; roses first flower at 2-5 yr; seed dormancy 12-15 months)

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS Rosa arkansana (flowers May-Aug, 5-petalled pink, in clusters or solitary; hips 10-15 mm in clusters of 2-3, 15-30 achenes each); hips persist into winter as in most wild roses; hips eaten raw (vitamin C)

shrub.name: New Jersey tea
shrub.source: Ceanothus americanus, eastern and central North America, low shrub 0.5-1 m of dry prairie, oak savanna and open woods with a huge red burl-like root, white flower clusters in early summer — USDA FEIS / Flora of North America

leaf.note: three prominent veins curving from the base to the tip; finely toothed; downy beneath

shrub.silhouette: low rounded shrub foamed with white flower puffs

growth.juvenile_note: Hard seeds sprout after fire or scarification. The seedling is a thin stem with a few toothed, three-veined leaves that puts most of its effort into a deep, thick reddish root; for years it stays a few small stems, dying back and resprouting from the root crown after fire, and builds into a low many-stemmed bush whose root may be a gnarled burl as big as a fist.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Ceanothus americanus (seed dormancy broken by heat and scarification; sprouts from a massive root crown after fire; shrub 0.3-1 m; flowers on current-year shoots). Age at first flowering and lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: Flora of North America / USDA FEIS Ceanothus americanus (white flowers in dense rounded clusters on long stalks, May-Jul; three-lobed capsules that split explosively and fling the seeds). Fruit set and crop estimated.

bark.notes: thin green to reddish-brown stems from a woody root crown; dies back after fire

leaf.notes: ovate toothed leaves with three strong curving veins, soft-hairy beneath

flower.form: small white flowers in fluffy rounded clusters on long stalks above the leaves

fruit.form: small three-lobed dark capsules that crack open in late summer

appearance.silhouette: knee-high shrub dotted with white puffs among prairie grass
appearance.refs: USDA FEIS; Flora of North America; Missouri Botanical Garden

shrub.name: Smooth sumac
shrub.source: Rhus glabra, the only shrub native to all 48 contiguous US states, 1-4 m clonal thickets on prairie edges, old fields and roadsides; scarlet in autumn with upright red fruit clusters — USDA FEIS / Kew POWO

leaf.note: long pinnate leaves of lance-shaped toothed leaflets, whitish beneath; scarlet in autumn

shrub.silhouette: flat-topped clonal thicket, scarlet in autumn

growth.juvenile_note: Hard-coated seeds sprout mostly after fire or long weathering. The seedling is a single stout, smooth stem with a few large compound leaves; within a few years it sends out shallow roots that sucker up new stems all around, so a single seedling becomes a dome-shaped colony, tallest in the middle, of sparsely branched stems with leaves crowded at the tips.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Rhus glabra (shrub 1-3 m, rarely 6 m; spreads by rhizomes into clones; seed coat dormancy broken by fire or scarification; stems short-lived, clones persist; shade-intolerant). Stem ages estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS Rhus glabra (dense terminal panicles of small yellow-green flowers in June-July, mostly dioecious, bee-pollinated; dense upright clusters of hairy red drupes 4-5 mm ripen Aug-Sep and persist into winter, a famine food for birds; sour fruit used for a lemonade-like drink). Crop estimated.

bark.notes: smooth grey-brown stems with scattered lenticels; stout pithy twigs with a bluish bloom

leaf.notes: long feathery compound leaves of toothed lance-shaped leaflets, whitish beneath

flower.form: small yellow-green flowers in dense upright cone-shaped clusters

fruit.form: dense upright cone of velvety dark red berries held above the leaves into winter

appearance.silhouette: flat-topped thicket of bare stems with red fruit cones on a prairie edge

ground.name: Big bluestem
ground.source: Andropogon gerardii, dominant tallgrass prairie grass, central N America, 1.5-2.5 m, turns bronze in autumn — USDA PLANTS

traits.native_range: Andropogon gerardii, dominant tallgrass prairie grass, central N America, 1
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

ground.silhouette: tall blue-green grass, turkey-foot seed heads

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: a thin first blade; the first season it stays a small tuft of a few flat blue-green leaves while roots grow deep. Short rhizomes then thicken the clump year by year; in late summer it sends up stout purple-bronze stems to 3 m topped by three-branched 'turkey-foot' seed heads, and the foliage turns copper-red in autumn.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Andropogon gerardii: leaves 0.75-0.9 m by midsummer, flower stalks to 3 m, flowering Jul-Sep; leaves function at 5-10% of full sun (shade tolerant); clones may live for centuries. USDA NRCS plant guide: emergence in ~4 weeks with irrigation; first-season growth slow, faster from rhizomes later; full sun or partial shade. Clump age and first seed estimated.

ground.name: Field dog-lichen

growth.juvenile_note: No seedling: a new thallus starts from a broken lobe or a spore that meets a free-living cyanobacterium. It begins as a small grey scale on bare soil between grass clumps and grows outward as broad rounded lobes a few millimetres to a centimetre a year, the edges curling up and turning whitish and felted; older lobes overlap into a rosette a hand across.
growth.source: Brodo, Sharnoff & Sharnoff, Lichens of North America (thallus to ~10 cm, lobes 6-15 mm wide with upturned tomentose margins, cyanobacterial photobiont, on soil and moss over limestone and sand). Growth rate and ages estimated from Peltigera.

repro.note: no flowers: spreads by fragments and by spores that must meet a cyanobacterium; needs a wet film to grow, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Peltigera rufescens, Peltigeraceae: a foliose dog-lichen 3-10 cm across of grey-brown lobes with upturned felted margins and red-brown saddle-shaped fruit bodies, on dry calcareous and sandy soil in grassland and prairie — Brodo, Lichens of North America; Index Fungorum

leaf.notes: broad rounded lobes, grey to brown above (greener when wet), margins curled up and whitish-felted; underside white with a net of brown veins and root-like rhizines
